analysis.one_liner: Ends federal tax credits that pay oil companies to pump carbon dioxide into wells to recover more oil.
analysis.headline: Referred to the House Ways and Means Committee with 12 Democratic cosponsors and no action since introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would close two federal tax loopholes that subsidize enhanced oil recovery, the process of injecting captured carbon dioxide into aging oil fields to push out more crude. One change bars new projects from claiming the 45Q carbon capture credit for using CO2 as an oil-recovery agent; the other repeals the older Section 43 enhanced oil recovery credit outright. Both changes apply to tax years after enactment, and both are Ways and Means Committee referrals with no further movement.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently fund a per-ton credit for CO2 used to produce more oil, and the public, which bears the climate cost of that extra production. Existing storage-only carbon capture projects are unaffected, and the credits for genuinely permanent CO2 storage would remain in place.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near oil fields

how_it_helps.text: The bill ends the ability of new facilities to claim the 45Q carbon oxide credit for using CO2 as a 'tertiary injectant' in oil fields, the use the 45Q credit pays for even though the CO2 is being deployed to extract more crude [S2].
It repeals Section 43 of the tax code, the long-standing enhanced oil recovery credit, entirely, along with the conforming references to it scattered through the code [S2].
The changes apply to tax years beginning after enactment, so a future flow of federal tax dollars to oil extraction would stop rather than phase out slowly [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers, particularly those operating mature fields that depend on CO2 injection, and carbon capture developers who planned to finance projects by selling CO2 to oil fields rather than storing it permanently. Existing facilities are grandfathered under the bill's effective date, so current claimants keep their credits.

drawbacks.text: Eliminating the oil-recovery pathway under 45Q removes a major revenue stream that carbon capture projects have used to finance themselves; some projects that would have captured and injected CO2 may not get built at all, even though most of the CO2 used in enhanced oil recovery stays underground [S2].

The bill only affects credits for oil recovery; the much larger 45Q credits for permanent CO2 storage remain untouched, so its fiscal and climate impact is narrower than the 'polluter welfare' framing suggests [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core case is straightforward: the federal government should not pay a per-ton reward for CO2 whose purpose is producing more oil. The cost side is real but modest — the change applies only to facilities not yet built, and the bill preserves the storage-based credits that most carbon capture advocates want to keep. The main honest objection is that stripping the oil-revenue pathway could make some carbon capture projects financially unworkable, but a subsidy that rewards oil production is a poorly targeted way to achieve that goal.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in late March 2026 and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which has taken no action on it since, so it sits without a hearing or vote as the Congress continues.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the bill on March 26, 2026, joined by eight original cosponsors including Reps. Tlaib, Jayapal, and Schakowsky [S2].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and the action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor vote since [S4].
Twelve House Democrats have cosponsored the bill, all members of the majority-seeking or progressive wing of the caucus, with no Republican cosponsors [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: If the bill remains stalled, oil producers and enhanced-oil-recovery operators keep billions in existing tax credits that the bill would have ended, and Ways and Means's jurisdiction over tax legislation means no action can happen without the committee taking it up.

industries.industry: Enhanced oil recovery operators and oil producers using CO2 injection
industries.note: These operators currently collect a per-ton federal tax credit for injecting CO2 into oil fields, which pays them while producing more crude. The bill ends that credit for future facilities and repeals the older Section 43 EOR credit outright.
Projects that store CO2 permanently keep their 45Q credits, but developers who planned to sell captured CO2 to oil fields to make projects pencil out lose that financing pathway for new facilities.

analysis.trajectory: A tax bill with 12 cosponsors, all from one party, referred to Ways and Means in an election-year Congress, has no realistic path to a markup or floor vote this session. It will most likely die at the end of the Congress like most private member tax bills, unless it is attached to a larger tax package, which is unlikely given its narrow, industry-specific scope.
